title: Evaluating LLM apps
summary: Measure whether your LLM app actually works — build test sets, define metrics, and grade outputs with code and with an LLM judge.
objectives: Explain why LLM apps need evaluation, not just spot-checking
Build a small, representative evaluation dataset with inputs and expected outputs
Choose metrics that fit the task: exact match, similarity, or rubric scores
Write code-based (deterministic) checks for structured outputs
Use an LLM-as-judge to grade open-ended responses against a rubric
Track results over time so you can catch regressions before users do

quiz.q: Why is spot-checking a few prompts by hand a poor way to evaluate an LLM app?
quiz.answer: It isn't repeatable or representative — small manual checks miss edge cases, can't catch regressions when you change the prompt or model, and don't give you a number you can track over time.
quiz.why: Evaluation needs a fixed dataset and a metric so results are comparable across changes.

quiz.q: Which metric is the right fit for grading a classifier that must output exactly 'positive', 'negative', or 'neutral'?
quiz.why: A fixed label set has one correct answer per item, so exact match against the expected label is simplest and most reliable.

options: Letting the model pick its own training data
Using a second LLM call to grade an output against a rubric
A tool that auto-fixes failing tests
quiz.why: For open-ended answers there's no single correct string, so you prompt a model to score the output against explicit criteria.

quiz.q: When you change your prompt and your eval accuracy drops from 0.92 to 0.78, what has happened?
options: A regression — the change made the app worse on your test set
quiz.why: A drop on a fixed test set is a regression; catching it before shipping is the whole point of evals.

quiz.q: Give one reason to prefer a code-based check over an LLM judge when both could work.
quiz.answer: Code-based checks are deterministic, free, and instant — so for structured or exact-match outputs they're cheaper and more reliable than spending a model call to judge.
quiz.why: Use the LLM judge only where there's no programmatic ground truth, like tone or open-ended quality.

quiz.q: Why should your evaluation dataset be kept separate from the examples you use to design the prompt?
quiz.answer: So you measure generalisation, not memorisation — if you tune the prompt on the same examples you grade on, a high score may just mean you overfit to those cases.
quiz.why: A held-out test set gives an honest estimate of how the app behaves on unseen inputs.

body_markdown:
## Why evaluate at all?

When you build an ordinary program, you write tests: given an input, you assert the exact output. LLM apps are harder — the same prompt can give slightly different wording each time, and "correct" is often a matter of degree. But that does **not** mean you skip measuring. It means you measure deliberately.

Without evaluation you are flying blind. You tweak a prompt, it *feels* better, you ship it — and you've quietly broken three other cases. An **evaluation** (an "eval") turns "feels better" into a number you can compare.

## The three ingredients of an eval

Every eval has the same shape:

1. A **dataset** — a list of inputs paired with what a good answer looks like.
2. A **task** — the function that runs your app on each input.
3. A **metric** — a rule that scores each output, giving you one number overall.

Keep the dataset small but representative: 20–50 hand-picked cases that cover the easy path *and* the tricky edges. And hold it back — don't tune your prompt on the very examples you grade on, or you're just memorising.

## Picking a metric

Match the metric to the task:

- **Exact match** — for fixed outputs like classification labels. Did the model output exactly `positive`?
- **Similarity** — for short factual answers where wording varies; compare against the expected answer.
- **Rubric score** — for open-ended text (a summary, an email). Here there is no single right string, so you grade against explicit criteria.

## Code-based checks

Whenever there's a programmatic ground truth, check it with code — it's free, instant, and deterministic. Here we grade a sentiment classifier built on the Claude Messages API.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

dataset = [
    {"text": "I love this!", "label": "positive"},
    {"text": "This is terrible.", "label": "negative"},
    {"text": "It arrived on Tuesday.", "label": "neutral"},
]

def classify(text):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5",
        max_tokens=10,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"Reply with one word — positive, negative, or neutral:\n{text}"}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text.strip().lower()

correct = sum(classify(row["text"]) == row["label"] for row in dataset)
print(f"Accuracy: {correct / len(dataset):.2f}")
```

## LLM-as-judge

For open-ended outputs there's no string to match, so you ask a *second* model call to grade the answer against a rubric. Use a clear rubric and force a numeric score so you can average it.

```python
def judge(question, answer):
    rubric = (
        "Score 1-5 how accurate and helpful the answer is. "
        "Reply with ONLY the integer."
    )
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=5,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"{rubric}\n\nQ: {question}\nA: {answer}"}],
    )
    return int(msg.content[0].text.strip())

score = judge("What is the capital of France?", "Paris is the capital of France.")
print(f"Judge score: {score}/5")
```

## Track it over time

Save each run's score next to the prompt and model you used. The moment a change drops the number, you've caught a **regression** before your users did. That single habit — a held-out dataset, a metric, a recorded score — is what separates a hobby prompt from a production LLM app.

## Your task

Build a tiny `evals/` folder for one of your own prompts: a `dataset.jsonl` with 10 cases, and a script that prints one accuracy or average-score number.

slides.title: Evaluating LLM apps
slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we tackle a skill that separates people who tinker with prompts from people who ship real A I products: evaluation. By the end you'll know how to build a test set, pick a sensible metric, grade outputs with code and with an L L M judge, and track your results so you catch problems before your users do.

slides.title: Why evaluate?
bullets: Same prompt can give different wording.
"Feels better" is not a measurement.
A tweak can silently break other cases.
An eval turns a feeling into a number.
slides.narration: With ordinary code you write a test and assert an exact answer. L L M apps are messier: the same prompt can phrase things differently each time, and correct is often a matter of degree. But that doesn't mean you skip measuring. Without an eval you tweak a prompt, it feels better, you ship it, and you've quietly broken three other cases. An evaluation turns feels better into a number you can actually compare.

slides.title: Three ingredients of an eval
bullets: Dataset: inputs paired with good answers.
Task: the function that runs your app.
Metric: a rule that scores each output.
slides.narration: Every eval has the same three parts. First, a dataset: a list of inputs paired with what a good answer looks like. Second, a task: the function that runs your app on each input. Third, a metric: a rule that scores each output and rolls up to one number. Get these three right and the rest is mechanical.

slides.title: Build a good dataset
bullets: 20-50 hand-picked, representative cases.
Cover the easy path and the tricky edges.
Hold it back — don't tune on it.
slides.narration: Keep the dataset small but representative. Twenty to fifty hand-picked cases that cover the normal path and the awkward edges is plenty to start. And here's the crucial rule: hold it back. Don't tune your prompt on the very examples you grade on, or you're just memorising those cases and your score will lie to you. A held-out set tells you how the app behaves on inputs it hasn't seen.

slides.title: Pick a metric
bullets: Exact match — fixed labels.
Similarity — short factual answers.
Rubric score — open-ended text.
slides.narration: Match the metric to the task. For fixed outputs like classification labels, use exact match: did the model output exactly positive? For short factual answers where wording varies, compare similarity against the expected answer. And for open-ended text like a summary or an email, there's no single right string, so you grade against an explicit rubric. Choosing the wrong metric is the most common eval mistake.

slides.title: Code-based checks
bullets: Use when there's a programmatic answer.
Free, instant, and deterministic.
Grade against the expected label.
slides.narration: Whenever there's a programmatic ground truth, check it with code. It's free, it's instant, and it's deterministic. Here we call the Claude Messages A P I with the fast Haiku model to classify some text, then later we'll compare its answer to the expected label. Notice we never paste an A P I key into the code — the client reads it from an environment variable called ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY.

slides.title: Scoring accuracy
bullets: Run the task over every row.
Count how many match the label.
Divide to get one number.
slides.code:
correct = sum(
    classify(r["text"]) == r["label"]
    for r in dataset
)
acc = correct / len(dataset)
print(f"Accuracy: {acc:.2f}")
slides.narration: Scoring is then simple arithmetic. We run the classifier over every row, count how many outputs match the expected label, and divide by the total. That gives one accuracy number between zero and one. Run this every time you change the prompt or the model, and you'll instantly see whether you helped or hurt.

slides.title: LLM-as-judge
bullets: For open-ended answers with no exact match.
A second model call grades the output.
Use a clear rubric, force a numeric score.
slides.code:
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=5,
    messages=[{"role":"user",
        "content": f"{rubric}\nQ:{q}\nA:{a}"}],
)
score = int(msg.content[0].text.strip())
slides.narration: For open-ended outputs there's no string to match, so we ask a second model call to grade the answer. This is called L L M as judge. We give it a clear rubric — here, score one to five for accuracy and helpfulness — and we force it to reply with only the number, so we can parse it and average it. Use a capable model like Sonnet for judging, and only reach for it when code can't do the job.

slides.title: Code check or LLM judge?
bullets: Programmatic answer → code check.
Tone or open quality → LLM judge.
Code is cheaper and never flaky.
slides.narration: So which do you use? If there's a programmatic answer — a label, an exact value, valid Jason — use a code check. It's cheaper and never flaky. Reserve the L L M judge for things code can't measure, like tone, helpfulness, or open-ended quality. A good eval suite usually mixes both: deterministic checks where possible, a judge where necessary.

slides.title: Track it over time
bullets: Record score, prompt, and model together.
A drop on a fixed set is a regression.
Catch it before users do.
slides.narration: The final habit ties it all together. Save each run's score next to the prompt and the model you used. Then the moment a change drops the number on your fixed dataset, you've caught a regression — before it reached a single user. That discipline, a held-out dataset plus a metric plus a recorded score, is exactly what makes an L L M app production-ready rather than a lucky prompt.

Match the metric to the task.
Code checks first, LLM judge when needed.

slides.narration: Let's recap. An eval is three things: a dataset, a task, and a metric. Match the metric to the task — exact match, similarity, or a rubric. Prefer cheap deterministic code checks, and bring in the L L M judge only for open-ended quality. And always record your score so you catch regressions early.
